identification.summary: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM) is a China-linked cyberespionage actor that first became known for compromising telecommunications providers by exploiting unpatched internet-facing services such as WildFly/JBoss, then deploying web shells and off-the-shelf credential and lateral-movement tools [S1]. Unit 42 reported in 2022 that the group had expanded beyond telecommunications to financial institutions and government entities and was using a new RAT, PingPull [S2]. In 2023 reporting tied the same cluster (Alloy Taurus) to a Linux PingPull variant and a new backdoor, Sword2033, and to intrusions against a Southeast Asian government [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE describes GALLIUM as active since at least 2012 [S5]. Cybereason's Operation Soft Cell evidence pointed to activity since at least 2017, possibly linked to activity from 2012 [S6]. Microsoft's 2019 report covered activity observed mainly from 2018 to mid-2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM); press coverage of Unit 42's 2023 reporting states that Microsoft tracks Alloy Taurus/Gallium as Granite Typhoon [S3]. In Microsoft's taxonomy, 'Typhoon' denotes origin or attribution to China [S9]. Unit 42 tracks the group as Alloy Taurus and describes GALLIUM as also known as Softcell [S2][S3]. Microsoft and Cybereason describe the same activity under different names: Microsoft's GALLIUM and Cybereason's Operation Soft Cell [S1][S6]. MITRE tracks the group as GALLIUM (G0093) [S5].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (vendor assessment; no government attribution found in the sources gathered). MITRE describes GALLIUM as likely Chinese state-sponsored [S5]. Unit 42 says that the group's targeting, its focus, and its use of known Chinese threat-actor tools have led industry assessments to consider it likely a Chinese state-sponsored group [S2].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only, at 'likely' level [S2][S5]. Cybereason concluded that the Soft Cell operators were likely Chinese, based on tools such as Poison Ivy and China Chopper [S7]. Microsoft's 2019 GALLIUM report does not attribute the group to a specific state [S1]. Microsoft's later 'Typhoon' name signals China origin or attribution under its taxonomy [S9].
attribution.basis: Tooling overlap with known Chinese actors (China Chopper, Poison Ivy, PlugX-family and Gh0st-derived malware) [S1][S2][S7]; consistent targeting of telecommunications and government entities of strategic interest [S2]; infrastructure reused across operations and observed in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan [S1].

objectives: Intelligence collection from telecommunications providers. Cybereason assessed that the Soft Cell operators sought call detail records (time, duration, and source and destination numbers) for a small set of subscribers [S6]. Targeting later widened to government and financial entities, consistent with broader espionage [S2][S4].

regions: Southeast Asia, Europe and Africa (historic telecom targeting) [S2]
Afghanistan, Australia, Belgium, Cambodia, Malaysia, Mozambique, the Philippines, Russia and Vietnam (entities linked to 2022 infrastructure) [S2]
South Africa and Nepal (2023 Linux PingPull/Sword2033 activity) [S3]
Middle East telecommunications providers (2023 Soft Cell-linked activity reported by SentinelLabs; see gaps) [S8]
targeting.notes: Telecommunications has been the most consistent focus [S1][S2]. Unit 42's 2022 country list comes from targeted entities tied to GALLIUM infrastructure, not from confirmed compromises [S2]. A 2023 C2 domain mimicked a South African military domain but was not directly tied to the South African government [S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is mainly through exploitation of unpatched internet-facing services, notably WildFly/JBoss, using public exploits [S1]. After access, the group installs web shells (China Chopper and BlackMould, an IIS variant derived from China Chopper) and relies on compromised domain credentials. Its common tools are HTRAN, Mimikatz, NBTScan, Netcat, PsExec, Windows Credential Editor and WinRAR [S1]. Malware includes modified Gh0st-variant QuarkBandit and Poison Ivy RATs, altered to evade signatures, and SoftEther VPN for persistence [S1][S3]. At least one credential-dumping tool was signed with a stolen code-signing certificate [S1]. PingPull (2022) is a RAT with variants that communicate over ICMP, HTTP(S) or raw TCP. Its ICMP use exploits the limited inspection of ICMP on most networks [S2]. In 2023 the group added a Linux PingPull variant (detected by only 3 of 62 antivirus engines at the time) and the Sword2033 ELF backdoor for file transfer and command execution [S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Soft Cell
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reported a worldwide campaign against telecommunications providers, with evidence of activity since at least 2017, aimed at call detail records for selected subscribers.

campaigns.name: GALLIUM telecom intrusions
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported GALLIUM exploiting WildFly/JBoss and using web shells, Mimikatz, PsExec and modified Poison Ivy and Gh0st-variant malware against telecommunications providers, mainly from 2018 to mid-2019.

campaigns.name: PingPull expansion
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported a new PingPull RAT and expansion to government and finance targets, with infrastructure linked to entities in nine countries.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government intrusions
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 attributed intrusions against a Southeast Asian government, beginning in early 2022, to Alloy Taurus.

campaigns.name: Middle East telecom intrusions (Soft Cell-linked)
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs reported Middle Eastern telecommunications providers targeted in activity linked to Operation Soft Cell, with initial access through internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers. Cluster linkage to Granite Typhoon is not confirmed by Microsoft.

campaigns.name: Linux PingPull and Sword2033
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported a Linux PingPull variant and the new Sword2033 backdoor used against targets in South Africa and Nepal.

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage operators; vendors assess them as likely state-sponsored [S2][S5]. No named individuals or units appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Public exploits for internet-facing servers; China Chopper and BlackMould web shells; Mimikatz, WCE, PsExec and HTRAN; modified Poison Ivy and QuarkBandit; PingPull (Windows/Linux) and Sword2033 [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Dynamic DNS C2 subdomains (e.g., under ddns.net and myftp.biz); Taiwan-based servers for web shell connections; GALLIUM-exclusive IPs reused across operations [S1]; a C2 domain mimicking a South African military domain [S3]; SoftEther VPN inside victim networks [S1].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications providers, government entities and financial institutions in Southeast Asia, Europe, Africa and elsewhere [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Telecom metadata collection (call detail records of selected subscribers) supports surveillance of individuals of interest [S6]; government targeting supports broader intelligence requirements [S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing application servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) and weak ICMP inspection [S1][S2][S8].

gaps: Primary Unit 42 reports (2022 PingPull, 2023 Linux PingPull, 2023 SE Asian government) could not be fetched; facts come from search-result coverage and secondary press [S2][S3][S4].
Microsoft's threat-actor naming table (learn.microsoft.com) could not be opened; the Granite Typhoon = GALLIUM mapping relies on press coverage of Unit 42 reporting [S3].
The Cybereason Operation Soft Cell primary report was not opened; details come from GovInfoSecurity and Virus Bulletin coverage [S6][S7].
SentinelLabs' 2023 Middle East telecom activity is described as linked to Soft Cell. Whether Microsoft attributes it to Granite Typhoon, rather than another China-nexus cluster, is unverified [S8].
The CrowdStrike alias PHANTOM PANDA and the 'Red Dev 4' alias in the imported record were not confirmed in any source gathered.
No government attribution, indictment or sanctions naming this group was found; sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is unknown.
Activity after 2023 was not found in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Telecom provider networks hold call detail records, and internet-facing application servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) at telecom, government and finance entities are key terrain [S1][S2][S6][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched public-facing services give a no-interaction foothold, and ICMP-based C2 can evade networks that do not inspect ICMP [S1][S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit a public-facing server, then install a China Chopper or BlackMould web shell, harvest credentials with Mimikatz or WCE, move laterally with PsExec, persist through RATs (PingPull, Poison Ivy) or SoftEther VPN, and stage data with WinRAR [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained, low-cost collection of subscriber metadata and government data from telecom and government networks [S1][S4][S6]. MDCOA is wider access to partner-nation telecom infrastructure that supports surveillance of persons of interest to US or partner forces [S6]. Candidate indicators: web shells on IIS or JBoss servers; anomalous ICMP payloads; SoftEther VPN on servers; dynamic DNS C2 (ddns.net, myftp.biz); tools signed with stolen certificates [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track exploitation of internet-facing servers and ICMP C2 patterns across DoD-adjacent and partner telecom networks the group has targeted (Southeast Asia, Africa, Europe) [S1][S2]. Authorities: much of the targeted terrain is commercial or partner-nation telecom outside the DODIN, so response depends on coordination with partner nations and private providers rather than direct DoD action [S2][S6]. Mission assurance: communications transiting compromised partner telecoms may expose metadata on deployed personnel; plan for that risk [S6]. Coordination: share indicators (web shells, PingPull, dynamic DNS C2) with partner CERTs and commercial providers, and reconcile vendor naming (GALLIUM, Alloy Taurus, Softcell) in shared reporting [S1][S2][S3].
